newsitem.title: UK: Dollar rallies despite Bundesbank attack.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rallies despite Bundesbank attack.

text.p: The dollar rallied on Wednesday despite a fresh attack from the German Bundesbank, but European bourses were unable to find much life and turned lower with Wall Street.
Both French and German shares fell as Wall Street failed to match Tuesday's record-breaking performance when it rose 78 points.
The Dow Industrials average dropped 25 points in the first 30 minutes of trade, dragging London off its highs although it remained the only major market in Europe to show gains on the day.
New York traders said the Dow dropped in tandem with bonds on profit-taking following Tuesday's late surge.
Analysts said a lower than forecast January consumer inflation number was partially offset by a larger than forecast December international trade deficit.
U.S. consumer prices rose only 0.1 percent in January, the smallest monthly increase since last summer, after rising 0.3 percent in December.
Analysts have been suprised that inflation has remained largely contained even though the U.S. economic expansion is one of the longest since World War Two and shows no signs of a serious weakening.
The U.S. data had relatively little impact on the dollar, which appeared capped at around 1.6950 marks.

The Bundesbank helped drive the dollar during the morning after the central bank launched a fresh attack on the U.S. currency but at the same time made clear the mark's fall was having a positive impact on the German economy.
In its February monthly report, the Bundesbank said the mark appreciation seen in early 1995 -- when the dollar fell to an all-time low of 1.3438 marks -- had now been more than reversed.
But the bank acknowledged the dollar's strength had also had a positive impact on the German economy -- boosting its exports -- and had so far had no negative impact on inflation.
By 1515 GMT the dollar was quoted at 1.6933 marks and 124.05 yen compared with 1.6904 marks and 123.94 yen in late European trading on Tuesday.
Sterling clawed back some of Tuesday's sharp losses, gaining four pfennigs after receiving a boost from higher-than-expected retail sales. By 1515 GMT it was quoted at 2.7326 marks.
January retail sales rose by 0.6 percent month-on-month against forecasts for a 0.3 percent rise and scored a year-on-year rise of 4.6 percent against forecasts for a 3.9 percent increase.

"There is fairly robust underlying growth in retail sales still. So the theory that things are beginning to slow down, which in our view has always been exaggerated, may not be right," said Robert Prior, economist at HSBC James Capel.
The Italian lira had a rocky ride once more, falling to a three-month low near 1,000 per mark in early trade before recovering to 995.65 by 1515 GMT, up on late Tuesday's 996.73.

It was helped by Prime Minister Romano Prodi's announcement of a mini-budget which he said would enable Italy to meet the criteria for monetary union (EMU). Fears that Italy might miss the first wave of EMU have buffeted the lira in recent days.
In contrast to French and German share markets, London opened higher but pared its gains as Wall Street opened lower.
The blue chip FTSE 100 index was trading off its highs at 4,345 points for a gain of nearly 13 points by mid-afternoon.
"We are toying with all-time highs and we could be squeezed a bit higher short-term with the cash that's out there," said the head of equity trading at one leading brokerage.

Bank stocks were in focus again after Goldman Sachs downgraded Barclays shares following results at the low end of expectations. Barclays was down another 17 pence at 11.12 pounds after dropping 70-1/2p on Tuesday.
B.A.T Industries was up 18p at 546 after a surge in U.S. tobacco stocks amid renewed hopes that the industry is taking steps to settle its litigation problems, although B.A.T played down the reports.
German shares ended bourse trade sharply lower and slid further in later electronic dealing. The 30-share DAX index ended down 42.41 points, or 1.29 percent, at 3,233.75
The IBIS DAX index of screen-based trade was sharply lower at 3,213 points as market jitters in advance of Friday's options expiry and Wall Street's weak opening combined to drag the index lower.

"The downward pressure is coming more from the derivatives side than the retail side because of the expiry and this makes people more nervous. With futures traders things tend to move quickly, hence the rapid pace of change," one trader said.
French shares trimmed their losses after lower-than-expected U.S. inflation data. The CAC-40 index was down 22 points at 2,595 after recovering from a low of 2,586.
Thomson CSF rose 3.87 percent to 182.3 francs but was off its highs after the government announced the defence electronics firm would be sold by private sale.
CURRENCIES AT 1515 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6932 marks and 124.05 yen compared with 1.6904 marks and 123.94 yen in late European trading on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1515 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 13.8 points, or 0.32 percent, at 4,346.1
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 22.19 points, or 0.85 percent, at 2,595.33.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended down 42.41 points, or 1.29 percent, at 3,233.75. In later screen-based trade the IBIS-DAX index was down 17.48 at 3,213.35
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed in the afternoon at $346.25 an ounce after $346.10 at themonring fixing. Silver was barely changed at $5.19.
